```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE)
suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(SESSFclosures))
cl <- sf::st_drop_geometry(closures)
n_ver <- nrow(cl); n_cl <- length(unique(cl$closure_id)); n_now <- sum(is.na(cl$valid_to))
n_src <- nrow(instruments); n_pdf <- nrow(legislation)
```

This vignette records how the closure history in this package was prepared:
- the steps taken, from finding the legislation to releasing the package;
- the key instructions that shaped the work;
- what worked well, what was hard, and what we would do differently.

It is meant for anyone repeating a similar analysis for another fishery or
jurisdiction, or extending this one.

The work was done over two days (17–18 October 2026) by Paul Burch (CSIRO)
working with **Claude**, an AI assistant made by Anthropic (model Claude Opus
5.5), in the Claude Code desktop app on a Windows computer. Paul set the scope
and made the decisions. Claude:
- searched for the instruments;
- wrote and ran the R code (parser, assembly, package);
- drafted the documents.

Paul saw the results as they came and directed the next steps. A systematic
human check of the boundaries themselves is still to come (see
[Review status](#review)).

## Summary

| Step | Result |
|---|---|
| Find the legislation | `r n_src` source texts (instruments as made, and compilations) on the Federal Register of Legislation, May 2005 – June 2025 |
| Extract the text | Register HTML text of each instrument; the `r n_pdf` authorised PDFs, for page references |
| Parse the boundaries | A rule-based R parser turns the boundary descriptions into polygons |
| Dates in force | Commencement, revocation, cessation and compilation dates per instrument |
| Gear rules | Operative clauses classified into the gear each closure closes, and catch triggers |
| Assemble the history | `r n_cl` closures in `r n_ver` versions, `r n_now` in force now |
| Validate | Against AFMA's published polygons (2016 and 2021 directions) |
| Fill gaps | CAPAD polygons for parks defined only by State law |
| Document | HTML review document; list of questions for AFMA |
| Package | `SESSFclosures`: data, functions, tests, a self-contained rebuild in `data-raw/` |

## 1. Scoping

The work began as a side question in a session about ISMP strata. Paul asked
whether closure locations over time could be extracted from the legislation
"and summarise[d] … in both a document and a file of some kind [please
suggest the most appropriate type] that can be used for fisheries analyses",
and said not to start until he confirmed.

Claude proposed:
- **a GeoPackage**: one polygon per closure per period in force, with dates,
  gear, source and a quality flag; a vertex layer; a change log; and CSV/WKT
  copies for non-GIS users;
- **an R Markdown document** with maps, a timeline and page references.

A GeoPackage was chosen over shapefiles because it holds several layers and
long text fields in one file, and R (`sf`), Python (`geopandas`), QGIS and
ArcGIS all read it.

Two early decisions shaped the rest:
- **Start from the current instrument and work back.** The first pilot
  covered only the current compilation of the 2021 Closures Direction. The
  2016 and 2015 directions came next. Only after Paul's instruction to "go
  back as early as possible" did the scope become every instrument since
  2005.
- **Record provenance from the start.** Every polygon carries the instrument
  and schedule it came from, and a quality flag saying whether it is exact
  (coordinates only) or depends on an approximated feature.

## 2. Finding the legislation

- **No catalogue to start from.** The closures are written in "directions"
  made under the *Fisheries Management Act 1991*. Paul referred to "this
  site" without a link; Claude identified it as the Federal Register of
  Legislation.
- **First pass, by hand.** The current Closures Direction's versions page
  listed its compilations and amending instruments. The compilation's
  endnotes showed which schedules each amendment changed. Revocation clauses
  in each direction pointed to its predecessors.
- **Full catalogue, via the Register API.** For the full history the
  Register's API (`https://api.prod.legislation.gov.au/v1/`, OData) was
  searched by title ("closure", "SESSF", "Southern and Eastern Scalefish").
  That gave 52 instruments from SESSF Direction No. 01 (May 2005) on, with
  in-force dates and compilations (`data-raw/closures/R/14_catalogue.R`).
- **Pre-2005 instruments** were published in the Commonwealth Gazette and
  are not on the Register, so the history starts in 2005.
- **Text.** Each instrument's text came from the Register's HTML ("epub")
  view, which keeps the text in reading order. Tables are the exception: cells
  can be split over lines.
- **PDFs.** The authorised PDFs were downloaded later for page references
  (`21_fetch_pdfs.R`). Two URL patterns took trial and error, because the
  obvious page URL returns an empty web-app shell:
  - the API document endpoint;
  - `/{id}/{date}/{date}/text/original/epub/...` for compilations.

## 3. Parsing the boundary descriptions

A schedule describes each closure in words, for example:

> commencing at the intersection of the southern coastline of Kangaroo Island
> with the meridian of longitude 137° 16′ 59″ east; then south along that
> meridian to its intersection with the parallel of latitude 36° 00′ 00.8″
> south; … then westerly and northerly along the mean low water line to the
> point of commencement.

The parser (`fun_closures.R`, `fun_parse.R`) works in four stages.

**1. Split** each instrument into schedules, each schedule into areas, and
each area into clauses. Clauses are lettered items, "Then …" sentences, or
point-table rows.

**2. Read each clause** for three things:
- the point it reaches (latitude and longitude);
- the line it travels along: a parallel, meridian, geodesic, the coastline,
  the outer limit of coastal waters, a line *n* nautical miles seaward, the
  outer limit of the AFZ, or a State boundary;
- the feature the end point lies on.

**3. Resolve points that lie on a feature.** For example, "the intersection
of the coastline with the meridian 137° 16′ 59″ E". A meridian can cross a
coastline several times. The right crossing is chosen from, in order:
- the instrument's own words ("southern coastline of Kangaroo Island");
- the direction of travel ("generally north easterly");
- "close to" coordinates;
- a small gazetteer of named headlands ("in the vicinity of Cape
  Willoughby").

**4. Build the polygon** from the points, the feature-following segments
between them, circles ("a circle of radius 15 nautical miles"), islands
("a line 11 nautical miles seaward of … Island"), and exclusions. Then remove
land.

**Approximated features.** Features the instruments name but do not give as
coordinates are approximated (`03_features.R`):
- the coastline: ozmaps, plus Natural Earth for Lord Howe Island;
- *n* nm lines: buffers of the coastline;
- the outer limit of coastal waters: a 3 nm buffer with bay and gulf mouths
  closed (60 km closing, each landmass separately);
- the AFZ: a 200 nm buffer.

Every closure that uses one is flagged (`quality = "approx_feature"`).

**Drafting styles.** Twenty years of instruments use many styles. Each
variant below was found by building an instrument, finding the clauses that
failed, and extending the parser:

| Era | Drafting the parser had to handle |
|---|---|
| 2005 | degrees and minutes in words; decimal minutes labelled "seconds"; `''` as the seconds mark; whole degrees without a degree sign ("latitude 41 South"); a Symbol-font character as the degree sign |
| 2007–2013 | missing or swapped hemisphere words; "1nm"; "Thence" clauses; table cells (number, longitude, "E", latitude, "S") on separate lines; "until … intersects"; "beginning at"; "the point where the line began" |
| 2013 | the letter "o" as a degree sign; an apostrophe as the decimal point ("40'8″" = 40.8″); a 176-point table numbered in reverse |
| 2015–2018 | "Then" sentences; un-numbered latitude/longitude line pairs; "SCHEDULE N" with the title on the next line |
| 2021–2025 | consistent drafting; compilations without clause letters in the Register HTML |

Two clauses could not be read as written. They are corrected before parsing
by documented regular-expression fixes in `data-raw/closures/data/text_fixes.csv`
(see `text_fixes`). The coordinates are not changed.

## 4. Dates in force

`19_meta.R` sets each instrument's dates:
- **Start:** its commencement (stated in the text, or the day after
  registration).
- **End:** the earliest of three dates:
  - its repeal on the Register;
  - a stated cessation ("ceases to have effect after 1 January 2012");
  - the end of a stated period ("ending on 31 December 2006").
- **Compilations:** a compilation replaces the earlier text of its
  instrument from the compilation date.
- **Successors:** a direction revoked by its successor ends on the
  successor's commencement. The Register's date is a day later, which would
  otherwise make two consolidated directions overlap by one day.

This exposed a real gap: **no consolidated closures direction is on the
Register between 1 January and 12 July 2007**. Whether the closures lapsed
or were continued by other means is one of the questions for AFMA.

## 5. Gear rules and triggers

The operative clauses ("Fishing is not to be engaged in using trawl methods
in the areas described in Schedule 13, 40, 41, 42, and 44") were classified
into the gear each closure closes. Clauses that close an area only after a
catch trigger or other condition (dogfish triggers, the Small Pelagic Fishery
"evidence of benthic impacts" rule) are flagged as `trigger` and kept out of
the gear.

The classification was checked against gear tables made by hand for the 2015
and 2021 directions. Several bugs were found that way:
- Sentences naming several schedules were read only for the first schedule.
- Contents pages cut off the operative clauses.
- "Bounded by a line" was read as hook gear.

## 6. Assembling the history

`20_assemble_all.R` takes a snapshot of the areas in force on every date an
instrument starts or stops. It then links each area to the previous snapshot,
trying in order:
1. the same source text and name;
2. a similar name;
3. more than half overlap (intersection over union).

A new **version** starts when the boundary changes by 0.5 km² or more, or the
gear rule or trigger changes. A closure that lapses and returns within about
a year keeps its ID. The output is the GeoPackage, with layers for closures,
vertices, instruments, PDFs and pages, other measures, areas not mapped,
changes, and AFMA's polygons.

## 7. Validation

- **Within the legislation.** Each instrument was parsed independently, so
  successive instruments that restate a closure check each other: an
  unchanged closure should give the same polygon. Maps of the closures in
  force on selected dates were checked by eye, which caught several gross
  errors:
  - a coastline crossing taken on the north coast of Australia;
  - spikes from misread point tables;
  - depth closures missing their AFZ edge.
- **Against AFMA.** AFMA publishes polygons of the 2016 direction (one file
  per schedule) and the 2021 direction (a 2024 bundle). Both were downloaded
  with Paul's permission and compared:
  - Closures written wholly as coordinates match AFMA's to an
    intersection-over-union (IoU) of 0.98 or more.
  - The exception is Schedule 30, where AFMA's polygon has a spike that is not
    in the instrument.
  - Closures following approximated features agree to an IoU of 0.84–0.98.
    These are the best measure of how good the approximations are.
- **Other checks.** Areas were compared with gazetted figures where known.
  For example, the CAPAD marine parks: Kent Group 299 km² against 297 km²
  gazetted.

## 8. Filling the gaps

- **Parks defined only by State law.** The Kent Group National Park and the
  Victorian marine national parks are defined in the instruments by reference
  to State law, with no coordinates. Their polygons were taken from CAPAD 2022
  Marine (`quality = "capad_2022"`), with the caveat that they show the
  boundaries as at June 2022.
- **Questions for AFMA.** Problems found in the instruments were collected as
  questions for AFMA:
  - the 2007 gap;
  - a Western Isles position that falls on land;
  - Schedule 44 (2023) repeating Point 1;
  - the reversed 2013 table;
  - the Schedule 30 spike;
  - records of when trigger closures were triggered.

## 9. The R package

The package was built from the GeoPackage. Its parts:

| Part | Content |
|---|---|
| Data | `closures` and the supporting tables, as lazy-loaded data |
| Bundled files | the GeoPackage and the authorised PDFs, in `inst/` |
| Functions | `closures_on()`, `in_closure()` (shots inside a closure that applied to their gear), `closure_history()`, `closure_source()`, `closure_pdf()`, `gear_applies()`, `afma_polygons()`, `plot_closures()`, `review_status()` |
| Tests and checks | testthat tests; `R CMD check` |

Preparing it for public release on GitHub took these steps:
- a BSD 3-clause licence, with the bundled data's own terms in
  `inst/COPYRIGHTS`;
- a public README;
- removing every path to Paul's computer;
- making `data-raw/` self-contained, so `Rscript data-raw/run_all.R`
  rebuilds everything from the instrument texts. This was verified by
  rebuilding from a clean copy and comparing the result field by field;
- acknowledging Claude as a contributor;
- a record of the human review (below).

Building the package also improved the data: page-reference and gear-rule
bugs were found and fixed while writing tests and documentation.

## Key prompts

These are the instructions that most shaped the work, lightly abridged,
with what each led to.

| Prompt (Paul) | What it led to |
|---|---|
| "…are you able to extract the locations of closures over time from this site and summarise them in both a document and an file of some kind [please suggest the most appropriate type] that can be used for fisheries analyses" | Scoping; the GeoPackage and Rmd proposal. Asking Claude to *suggest* the format, and to wait for confirmation, gave a chance to agree the design first. |
| "…Write to the document, files and Claude.md regularly so you don't exceed the session limit or your context limit. I'm going to be away from my computer for a while, can you push notifications to the claude app on my phone please" | A progress log (`PROGRESS.md`) kept up to date throughout, which let the work survive context resets and a mid-run pause. Push notifications at milestones. |
| "Yes download the shape files and yes go back as early as possible" | Validation against AFMA, and the extension from 2015 back to 2005, the largest single expansion of scope. |
| "Also download all of the documents that contain the legislated boundaries and reference them, including page numbers of where the closure boundaries are specified" | The PDFs, `boundary_pages`, and `source_ref` on every closure. |
| "use CAPAD polygons for Kent Group and Victorian marine parks, draft an email to AFMA with the questions, create an R package with the closure details 'SESSFclosures'" | The CAPAD fill-in, the AFMA questions and this package. |
| "reword the README for public release, also please remove the paths to the files on my machine from the scripts in the package. Make it selfcontained" | The self-contained `data-raw/` rebuild, which in turn exposed the page-reference bug. |
| "Make sure Claude is appropriately acknowledged… Closure boundaries have yet to be checked by a human… perhaps in the NEWS file and we could update the package number to 1.0.0 when that happens" | The contributor entry, `NEWS.md`, the review log and `review_status()`. |
| "Does the package include the trawl closures that was implemented in south eastern Australia in 2023 or 2024?" | A spot check of a known recent change; it led to finding the incomplete page references. |

## What worked well

- **Working from the current instrument back.** The pilot on one compilation
  produced a usable result early and a parser that later instruments only
  needed to extend.
- **Independent builds as checks.** Each instrument is parsed on its own, so
  the many restatements of the same closure across 20 years act as built-in
  replicate measurements. Differences between successive builds were either
  real changes or parser bugs, and were easy to tell apart.
- **An external benchmark.** AFMA's polygons gave an objective accuracy
  measure. They also separated the two kinds of error: parsing errors, which
  should be zero for coordinate-only closures, and approximation error.
- **Provenance and quality flags on every row.** `source_ref`, `quality` and
  `notes` let users decide how far to trust each closure, and make review
  practical.
- **Maps of snapshots.** Plotting everything in force on a date caught gross
  errors that tables did not.
- **A written progress log and memory notes.** They allowed the work to
  continue across several context resets and a pause for a session limit.
- **Fixing drafting problems in data, not code.** Documented corrections
  (`text_fixes.csv`) keep unusual drafting visible and reviewable.
- **Asking before outward-facing steps.** Downloads from AFMA, publishing and
  sending email were confirmed with Paul first. The AFMA email was drafted,
  not sent, and GitHub publication was left to Paul.

## What was challenging

- **Drafting variation.** Most of the effort went into the long tail of
  drafting styles and typing errors in older instruments. Each fix risked
  breaking something that already worked. One did: allowing a schedule title
  to start with a digit, for the 2005 title "41 South", made cross-references
  like "Schedule 32." look like headings. The polygons were unaffected, but
  page references were wrong until a later full rebuild caught it.
- **Features with no coordinates.** The coastline, coastal waters and AFZ
  are defined in law by baselines and charts not available here. The
  approximations are the main source of error, and choosing the right
  coastline crossing needed several layered rules.
- **Linking areas over time.** Schedules are renumbered between directions,
  names change slightly, and a closure can be split, merged or lapse.
  Linking by source, then name, then overlap works, but the thresholds are
  judgement calls.
- **Dates.** Commencement and repeal are recorded inconsistently. The
  Register's end dates overlap successors by a day, older directions expire
  by stated period, and one gap (2007) may be real or an artefact of what is
  on the Register.
- **Gear rules.** The operative clauses are free text. Contents pages,
  conditional rules and multi-schedule sentences all caused misclassification
  that was found only when checking against hand-made tables.
- **Tooling on Windows.**
  - Paths over 260 characters.
  - Shell quoting: regular expressions passed through `sed`, PowerShell or
    `Rscript -e` were mangled more than once, so editing files directly was
    safer.
  - Spherical geometry in `sf` rejecting some approximated rings.
  - PDF and HTML text extraction giving different layouts of the same table.
- **Scale and context.** The work outgrew a single context window several
  times. Without the progress log, earlier decisions would have been lost.

## Advice for a similar analysis

1. **Agree outputs and provenance first.** Decide the output format, the
   unit of record (closure version) and the provenance fields before parsing
   anything.
2. **Build the catalogue from the API first.** List every instrument, its
   compilations and its in-force dates before parsing. Then the full scope
   and the dates are known up front, not found piecemeal.
3. **Get the external benchmark early.** If the agency publishes polygons,
   download them at the start and compare as each instrument is built. Ask
   the agency for its legal lines (coastal waters, AFZ) as well; that would
   remove most of the approximation error.
4. **Keep a regression suite from day one.** Record the expected area, or a
   checksum of each polygon, for every instrument already parsed, and rerun
   it after every parser change. The heading regression above would have been
   caught at once.
5. **Prefer data fixes for one-off drafting.** Keep the parser for patterns
   that recur, and put one-off oddities in a corrections table with a note.
6. **Map every snapshot.** Make a map of what was in force at regular dates
   and look at them as the work goes; it is the fastest check there is.
7. **Track page references and rules alongside geometry.** They are easy to
   neglect and need their own checks.
8. **Plan the human review as part of the work.** Use a per-version review
   log, a clear status flag, and a version number that only reaches 1.0.0
   after review.
9. **Keep one copy of the pipeline.** Here the scripts exist both in the
   original working folder and in the package's `data-raw/`. Keep only the
   package copy, or generate one from the other, so they cannot drift.
10. **Write progress down as you go.** With an AI assistant, a progress file
    and explicit instructions to update it let long jobs survive interruptions.
    Ask for notifications at milestones if you will be away.
11. **Spot-check with questions you already know the answer to**, such as "Is
    the 2023 Gabo closure there?". It is cheap and finds problems.

## Review status {#review}

Version `r utils::packageVersion("SESSFclosures")` has **not** had its
closure boundaries checked by a person (`review_status()`). The review will
be recorded closure by closure in `data-raw/closures/review/review_log.csv`
and described in `NEWS.md`, and the package will become version 1.0.0 when
it is complete.

```{r}
knitr::kable(review_status(), caption = "Closure versions by human review status.")
```
